newsitem.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia agrees to US proposal for Africa force.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia agrees to US proposal for Africa force.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Thursday that Ethiopia had become the second country to pledge troops for a proposed African crisis force to do peacekeeping.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi had promised to provide two battalions for the force, joining Mali in publicly signing on to the U.S.-led initiative.

Despite the concrete show of support from Ethiopia and Mali, Organisation for African Unity (OAU) Secretary General Salim Ahmed Salim said African leaders had concerns about the plan and pressed Christopher to respond.
Ethiopia, where he met separately with Salim and Zenawi, is Christopher's second stop on a five-nation African tour. He leaves Friday for Tanzania.

"The United Nations would have to take the decision to launch the mission and it would be under control of the United Nations as other peacekeeping endeavours, as other humanitarian endeavours," Christopher explained to envoys at OAU headquarters in Ethiopia.
But the mission would be "predominantly in the hands of those African countries that commited troops to the endeavour," he added, spelling out more detail on the still evolving force.
Salim, after private talks with Christopher, later called on the secretary to discuss African concerns publicly in connection with a speech Christopher gave to OAU ambassadors.
The 10,000-member all-African Crisis Response Force would be sent to countries where civil war, insurrection or campaigns of genocide threaten mass civilian casualties.
Salim said the U.S. plan is consistent with Africa's new willingness to seek African solutions to African problems.

But he also said the OAU had concerns, including why Washington only approached 10 of 47 sub-Saharan African states to join the force, who would command it, how long-term funding can be guaranteed and who would own the military equipment donated by the United States and other industrial nations.
South African President Nelson Mandela has also responded cautiously to the proposal that the two men will discuss on Saturday.
"Africa would like to feel that they are handling things themselves...not acting in response to suggestions that come from outside the continent," Mandela told Reuters.
OAU diplomats said it would cause problems if only states friendly to Washington joined and if the force was permanent.
Salim urged Washington to hold broader consultations and bring more African countries into the mix. U.S. officials want the force operational in about six months.
"It would not be a standing force but one that could be assembled quickly, led by Africans and deployed under U.N. auspices," Christopher promised the ambassadors.

Various ideas for a trained military force to act to prevent or respond to African crises have been proposed before. But frustrated by U.N. and OAU inaction, Washington seized the lead in organising and raising funds for the force.

Christopher said officials approached African countries who demonstrated interest, have experience in peacekeeping missions, civilian control over the military and "a sincere desire, not a mercenary desire" to be engaged.
Christopher has suggested the force would "help resolve conflicts in Africa and beyond."

As for funding, Christopher said this is being discussed with European and Asian allies because the administration believes there must be sustained support. But U.S. officials said they do not expect this to be a problem.
